summary.text: A position vector locates a point in space, using whichever coordinates and basis vectors are simplest for the task at hand.
Position vectors can be added and scaled in length, so the set of all of them forms a position space.
In an equation of motion, the position vector changes with time and defines where a particle is, and its time derivatives are used in kinematics.

facts.label: Fields that use it
facts.value: Differential geometry, mechanics and vector calculus

facts.label: Vector space operations
facts.value: Position vectors can be added and scaled

facts.label: Coordinate independence
facts.value: Different coordinates and basis vectors represent the same position vector

facts.label: Single parameter path
facts.value: One parameter describes a curved one-dimensional path

facts.label: Motion tracking
facts.value: The position vector r(t) defines a particle's motion

items.prompt: A weather model stores every location as an ordered list of readings, one for each direction a point can vary in. How many dimensions does its position space have?

options.label: One fewer than the length of that list.
Exactly the length of that list.
Always three, whatever the list holds.
Twice the length of that list.

items.explain: A position space has dimension n when each position is written as an n-tuple of coordinates, so the dimension matches the length of the list.

items.prompt: Two navigators track the exact same boat at sea using different grid maps. One uses rectangular grid lines while the other uses circular distance radar. How do their position vectors compare?

options.label: Both coordinate systems represent the exact same underlying position vector.
The radar coordinates shift the boat's physical location relative to the shore.
They produce two unrelated vectors pointing to different physical locations.
Rectangular grids are invalid for three-dimensional space while circular ones are valid.

items.explain: Different coordinate systems and their associated basis vectors still represent the exact same position vector.

items.prompt: Why is the set of all possible location vectors called a position space?

options.label: Because position vectors can only be multiplied together, never combined.
Because it can only exist in three-dimensional physical space.
Because all vectors in it are required to have a fixed length of one.
Because position vectors within it can be added together and scaled in length.

items.explain: The collection of position vectors forms a vector space because positions can be combined through vector addition and stretched or shortened through scalar multiplication.

items.prompt: Design software builds geometric shapes using mathematical parameters. If a software formula controls a position vector using two independent parameters, what shape does it generate?

options.label: A curved one-dimensional path.
A single stationary point.
A curved two-dimensional surface.
A curved three-dimensional volume.

items.explain: Parametrizing coordinates with one parameter creates a 1D path, two parameters describe a 2D surface, and three parameters describe a 3D volume.

items.prompt: An aerospace center tracks a rocket by updating its position vector continuously as time passes. What does this time-dependent vector construct?

options.label: A continuous path traced by the rocket as time values map to spatial locations.
A fixed reference point that cancels out the rocket's speed.
A static two-dimensional surface enclosing the rocket pad.
A change in coordinate axes without any movement of the object.

items.explain: Matching each successive value of time to a spatial coordinate sequence creates a continuous path traced by the moving point mass.

items.prompt: Engineers analyzing high-speed train stability calculate higher-order time derivatives of the train's position vector. What is the benefit of computing these extra derivatives?

options.label: They turn the position vector into a single scalar value without direction.
They eliminate the requirement for an origin point in physics calculations.
They force the position space to lose one of its dimensions.
They improve displacement approximations and allow representation as infinite sequence sums.

items.explain: Calculating higher-order derivatives improves approximations of displacement and lets engineers express motion functions as infinite series for analytical work.

paragraphs.heading: Where something is
paragraphs.text: A position vector says where something is. In an equation of motion, the position vector r(t) gives a particle's location relative to a chosen coordinate system at a time t, where a particle means a point mass. The term turns up mostly in differential geometry and mechanics, and now and then in vector calculus. It is usually used in two or three dimensions, but it extends easily to spaces with any number of dimensions.

paragraphs.heading: Many ways to name one place
paragraphs.text: In three dimensions, any set of coordinates and matching basis vectors can be used to locate a point, so you pick whichever is simplest for the job. These different choices all describe the same position vector. In fields such as continuum mechanics and general relativity, more general curved coordinates are used instead, and general relativity needs an extra coordinate for time.

paragraphs.heading: Position space
paragraphs.text: Position vectors can be added together and stretched or shrunk, and the result is always another position vector. That is why the set of all of them forms position space, a vector space whose members are position vectors. Each coordinate xᵢ can take any value, and a full list of values marks out a point. That list is called the coordinate vector or n-tuple (x₁, x₂, …, xₙ), and the number n is the dimension of the space.

paragraphs.heading: Curves, surfaces and volumes
paragraphs.text: Each coordinate can be made to depend on one or more parameters. With one parameter the coordinates trace a curved 1D path, with two a curved 2D surface, and with three a curved 3D volume. When position vectors describe a smooth curve in space, the parameter does not have to be time; it could be the length measured along the curve.

paragraphs.heading: From position to motion
paragraphs.text: To describe motion, let each coordinate depend on time. Each new moment then gives a new location, and if you imagine the moments packed infinitely close, those locations join up into the path the particle traces. This is why r(t) is usually the quantity people most want to find when solving an equation of motion: it pins down the whole motion.

paragraphs.heading: Rates of change
paragraphs.text: Because r depends on t, you can take its derivatives with respect to time. The first, second and third derivatives have standard names in basic kinematics, and they are widely used in kinematics, control theory and engineering. Higher derivatives can be found the same way, and studying them improves approximations of how an object is displaced. Such higher terms are needed to write the displacement accurately as an infinite sum, which opens up several methods in engineering and physics.
